title: Ashy Jutka
lines: Once upon a time there was a poor widow.
This woman had only one daughter, but she did not have much joy even in her.
This girl was so lazy that word of it spread beyond seven counties.
From morning till evening she sat in the ashes, poking at them,
stirring them with her fingers, and the village folk named her Ashy Jutka.
Oh dear, oh dear, how the poor widow fretted!
Being a widow was not enough, her daughter had to be lazy too.
All her kind words were in vain: you should work too, my daughter,
at something; at least spin one spindle of hemp a day!
She could talk all she liked: in one ear and out the other.
Then one day the poor woman ran out of patience,
she grabbed her distaff, with both hands, and gave Jutka a sound beating.
"There, take that!
Do you want more?"
Oh, how Jutka cried, the whole village rang with her crying, and she told her mother
that she would not beat her any more, because she was going out into the world.
"Go with God, and have a good road with no mud!"
Jutka did go, but as she stepped out into the street crying loudly,
who should come along but the prince in a coach with six horses.
He stopped the coach and asked the poor woman:
"Tell me, good mother, why did you beat your daughter?"
The widow answered:
"Because, if you please, I cannot get enough hemp for her,
she has already spun even the thatch of my garden shed, and she still wants to spin.
Too much of a good thing is too much!"
"Really, is this girl truly such a good spinner?"
said the prince, "then let her come to me, there is spinning for her there.
A great granary is full of hemp, and if she spins it all in one month,
here is my hand on it, I will make her my wife."
"Well now," thought the woman, "nothing will come of that,
but take her away!" The girl thought just the same,
but she got into the coach all the same, in case some wonder of the world might happen.
When they arrived at the king's palace,
the prince at once took Jutka into the granary.
He said:
"Now, Jutka, here you can spin as much as you like.
What I said, I said: if you spin in one month
all the hemp that is here, I will make you my wife."
Jutka could not even speak, she was so scared at the sight of that sea of hemp.
Why, she could not spin this in a thousand years.
She cried and grieved day and night.
One day passed after another, one week went by, then two,
then three, but not a single thread of the hemp was missing.
The little serving boy who brought her food asked when she would start spinning,
but Jutka only answered: there is still plenty of time for that.
But when she was alone in the granary, she cried like a rain shower.
How could she have been such a great fool as to sit down in the granary!
Soon the month would be over,
and the prince might even have her head cut off in his anger, for making a fool of him.
Just as she was thinking about this, all of a sudden,
good God knows from where, a teeny-tiny dwarf popped up in front of her.
But this dwarf had a beard seven yards long,
and wherever he went, he swept up the rubbish with his beard.
Jutka was scared: "Oh God, help me, what an ugly beast, what an ugly little man!"
But the dwarf spoke up:
"Good evening, Ashy Jutka!
I know what your trouble is.
Don't worry a bit, in one week I will spin every last thread
of the hemp that is here, and even wind it on the reel.
But then you must come with me."
"How can I go with you," said the girl, "when the prince has chosen me for himself?"
"Very well," said the dwarf, "I will not take you away if,
by the time I finish the spinning, you guess my name."
The girl thought: so be it.
It made no difference now which way her fate would turn.
She shook hands with the dwarf, and the bargain was made.
After that the dwarf came to the granary every night,
and he spun so fast that Jutka's eyes and mouth stood wide open in wonder.
What he spun by night he took away, and by day he reeled it in the forest branches.
When there was only one day left of the month,
the little serving boy came with supper, and Jutka asked:
"So what news is there outside, little serving boy?"
"Well, the news is that if you spin the hemp by tomorrow evening,
you will be the prince's wife."
"And didn't you hear anything else, little serving boy?"
"Yes, I did.
This afternoon I went hunting with the prince,
and as we wandered in the forest, we heard a clattering among the branches.
We looked up, and what did we see there?
A teeny-tiny dwarf with a beard seven yards long, just imagine!
He was reeling among the branches, and he kept saying:
I am Tirpe-Torpe Gyurka,
My wife will be Ashy Jutka.
The prince laughed loudly
at what that ugly little man was saying, and with that we went on."
Oh, how glad Ashy Jutka was to hear this!
Now she knew the dwarf's name.
The hemp would be spun, and still she would not have to go with the dwarf.
On the last evening the dwarf came and said to the girl:
"Now, Jutka, I have spun the hemp to the last thread, now come with me.
Or do you perhaps know my name?"
"Of course I know it," said Jutka, "your name is Tirpe-Torpe Gyurka."
In the morning came the prince, and the whole court with him.
Oh, how amazed they all were!
Everyone said that since the world began, no human eye had seen such a thing.
Even the old king said:
"Well, my son, until now I was against your marriage,
but now I say: only the spade, the hoe and the great bell shall part you two."
They held the wedding right away.
And what a wedding it was!
Everyone was there who was not late.
Everyone ate and drank who got something.
Two old women especially pushed about in vain, everything was eaten up before them.
So they went off to the prince to complain.
But even the prince had never seen two such ugly women.
One's eyelids, and the other's lips, hung down to the ground.
He asked them one after the other:
"Now why have your eyelids drooped down to the ground?"
"Because, my royal lord, I spun all my life,
and my eyes were always on the spindle."
"And why have your lips drooped down?"
he asked the other.
"That is because I licked the hemp a lot, so that I could spin more."
Oh, how frightened the prince was!
Why, then even his lovely wife might grow ugly like that.
So at once he forbade Jutka
ever again in her life even to hold a spindle in her hand.
And Jutka, believe it or not, obeyed, and she lives still, if she has not died.
